title: What are Sequenced Collections (Java 21: `SequencedCollection`/`SequencedSet`/`SequencedMap`, getFirst/getLast/reversed), and what gap did they fill?
shortTitle: What are Sequenced Collections (Java 21), and what gap did they fill?
keyPoints: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, and SequencedMap are three new interfaces in Java 21 that unify first, last, and reversed access for any ordered collection.
They add getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), addLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast(), and reversed() to the collection hierarchy.
List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap, and the sorted-set and sorted-map families were retrofitted to implement these interfaces.
The reversed() method returns a view, not a copy, so iterating it walks the original backwards and changes write through.
getFirst() and getLast() throw NoSuchElementException on an empty collection.
addFirst() and addLast() on a sorted set or map throw UnsupportedOperationException because position cannot override sort order.
The feature adds no new data structures; it is purely a unifying API that removes index arithmetic and iterator boilerplate.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sequenced Collections give every ordered collection one uniform API for first, last, and reversed access, filling the gap where getting the first or last element and reversing differed inconsistently across List, Deque, and ordered sets and maps.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`SequencedCollection`** – Base interface adding `getFirst()`, `getLast()`, `addFirst()`, `addLast()`, `removeFirst()`, `removeLast()`, and `reversed()` for any collection with a defined encounter order.
- **`SequencedSet`** – Extends `SequencedCollection` for sets with unique elements, refining `reversed()` to return a `SequencedSet`.
- **`SequencedMap`** – Map counterpart adding `firstEntry()`, `lastEntry()`, `pollFirstEntry()`, `pollLastEntry()`, `putFirst()`, `putLast()`, and `reversed()`.
- **Retrofitted** – `List`, `Deque`, `LinkedHashSet`, `LinkedHashMap`, and the `NavigableSet`/`NavigableMap` families now implement these interfaces.
- **`reversed()` view** – Returns a view, not a copy, so iterating walks backwards and changes write through to the original.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps several ordered queues: a line of customers at the counter, a ledger of transactions in date order, and a list of recent logins. Before Java 21, asking "who is first" and "who is last" worked differently for each: for one you called a method, for another you did size minus one, and for a set you had to iterate the whole thing just to reach the end. Sequenced Collections are like a single standard rule posted on every ordered queue: "to see the front, say getFirst; to see the back, say getLast; to read it backwards, say reversed."

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sequenced Collections, added in Java 21, are three new interfaces that give any collection with a defined encounter order one uniform API for first and last access and for reversal. SequencedCollection adds getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), addLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast(), and reversed(). SequencedSet refines this for unique elements. SequencedMap adds firstEntry(), lastEntry(), pollFirstEntry(), pollLastEntry(), putFirst(), putLast(), and reversed().

The gap they fill is that before Java 21, order was scattered across types with no shared interface. A List gave its first element with get(0) and its last with get(size() - 1). A Deque had getFirst() and getLast(). A LinkedHashSet had a defined iteration order but no direct way to reach the last element except iterating all the way to the end. There was no common type that said "I am ordered and I have a first and a last."

These interfaces were retrofitted into existing types, so List and Deque implement SequencedCollection, LinkedHashSet and the sorted-set family implement SequencedSet, and LinkedHashMap and the sorted-map family implement SequencedMap, all without changing declared types. The reversed() method returns a view rather than a copy, so iterating it walks the original backwards and changes through the view write back.

In banking work at National Bank of India this cleaned up ordered-collection code. A customer's transaction list exposed the most recent transaction with getLast() and a newest-first statement view with reversed(), instead of size-minus-one and manual reverse loops. A LinkedHashSet of recently used accounts gained direct first and last access. The senior details are that getFirst() and getLast() throw NoSuchElementException on an empty collection, and addFirst() or addLast() on a sorted set or map throws UnsupportedOperationException because position cannot override comparator order.

Remember one sentence: Sequenced Collections unify first, last, and reversed access across all ordered collection types with getFirst(), getLast(), and reversed(), eliminating inconsistent index arithmetic and iterator boilerplate.
